prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms made frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single prize part, and the first-round exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The chair's first question, whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave room, has a definite answer: the comb made optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize honoured control of individual trapped ions, but neither contains the magic-wavelength condition that cancels the light shift while many neutral atoms are held in a Lamb-Dicke lattice. That condition is what turned optical clocks from one-ion devices limited by quantum projection noise into instruments that average down in minutes, and it is why independent laboratories now compare Sr and Yb clocks at the 1e-18 level. As an instrument builder I regard that kind of verification, agreement between independently built devices, as the strongest available. On timing I would not wait for the redefinition of the second, which is a decision of metrology bodies and adds no scientific information. On credit, I read the pair as concept plus realization: Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group taking the platform to record accuracy and stability and into many-body clock physics. The citation should say invention and realization so both roles are stated. I do not see a case for widening to Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto or others without breaking the three-person limit and diluting a clean attribution.
statement.case_against: The reservation that still carries weight is that a reasonable reader can see the lattice clock as the third prize in one lineage of precision timekeeping, and Danielsson's point that this is a better way to make a measurement rather than a new observation about nature is a principled one, not a mere preference. The second is attribution at the edges: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Schmidt and the Paris, PTB and Boulder groups made real contributions, and two names will be read by some as unfair to them. Third, I am recalling the early strontium history from the supplied record and not from primary papers, so the exact division between Katori and Ye is not something I can settle beyond what the shortlist states. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and a prize ahead of it carries a small risk of looking early.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B038 and argues that the lattice clock is a refinement of precision timekeeping already honoured in 2005 and 2012, a better way of making one measurement rather than a new observation about nature, and that a result that changed understanding of electronic phases should rank ahead of it.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-engineering distinction seriously, but I do not think it separates these two entries as cleanly as you suggest. The lattice clock is not only a better measurement; its performance has opened new observations, namely clock-to-clock tests of relativistic redshift across millimetre scales, bounds on varying constants and dark-sector couplings, and many-body effects inside the clock itself. A prize for an invention whose capability keeps producing physics is within what the Prize has done before. I also share your worry about B038's credit chain, and your suggested wording around prediction and first observation does reduce it, but a citation cannot make Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang disappear from the story of why HgTe was the platform. That is the point on which I weigh B046 as cleaner.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first as a concept-level organising principle, the Z2 classification, confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi2Se3 for fifteen years, and notes that careful citation wording is needed because graphene's spin-orbit gap is too small for the original Kane-Mele model.
responses.response: Your argument for concept over instrument is the strongest case against my own preference, and I accept the maturity and the independence of the confirmations. Where I still differ is on what the committee would have to defend. Your own case_against concedes that the chain from prediction in graphene to realization in HgTe runs through a proposal by people outside the three names, and that the 2016 topological-phases prize will make some colleagues read this as a continuation. Those are two open questions the committee would have to answer in public. For B046 the open questions are the overlap with 2005 and 2012 and the timing, and I think the magic-wavelength argument answers the first. If the committee concludes that the clock is an advance of technique, I would support B038 as the next configuration, so my first alternative is unchanged.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042 as a falsifiable prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald) followed by the 2018 discovery, reproduced widely, and answers my opening rank of seventh by saying the citation need not rest on the pairing mechanism and that eight years is not unusual.
responses.response: You are right that a citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated states does not require the pairing mechanism, and I have moved to treat that as a real argument and not a dodge. I keep B042 as my second alternative for the first time on those grounds. My remaining difficulty is that your own case_against lists sample dependence and twist-angle disorder as limiting the cleanness of the phase diagram, and the experimental credit lands on one group while Cao and Fatemi, who did much of the measurement, and the earlier continuum-model authors fall outside three names. As a detector builder I am cautious about a field where the most important measurements are still being sorted into what is intrinsic and what is sample quality. I would reconsider in a few years; I do not think it is the right prize now.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the magic-wavelength idea is what neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize covered and says he would not widen the two-name credit, and in the chair's summary he raised his research stay in the Boulder laboratory of John Hall, where Ye's group is also based, and suggests the committee decide on recusal.
responses.response: We agree on the overlap argument and I have adopted your framing. On your Boulder point, a research stay in a different laboratory, with no documented collaboration or relationship with Ye or Katori, is a disclosure and not in itself a disqualification, and I would favour recording it and letting him vote while the committee notes it. I would not count it against the five explicit B046 supporters, because the other four arrive at the same preference from different backgrounds. The point on which I differ from you is tone toward the alternatives: I would not resist a second part just to be inclusive, but I would still resist one here, since no shortlisted partner for B046 has a credit set that stays within the three-person limit.

responses.point: Olsson moved B046 to the head of her configuration, and warns that a 2026 prize in precision measurement follows the 2025 circuit-physics award in the broader quantum-technology area, so the committee should not simply rotate toward the same community.
responses.response: I think the rotation worry is fair as a check, but it does not apply to this candidate. The 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electrical circuit, a condensed-matter system, whereas the lattice clock is atomic physics with a different community, different methods, and a different set of consequences in metrology and tests of fundamental physics. I would worry about rotation if B006 were leading, which it is not in anyone's preferred configuration. On the question of whether you regard the first-round ranking as spread too widely for B042, I agree that spread is not a substitute for judgement, and I have tried to weigh each candidate on the science and not on the count.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength, many-atom Lamb-Dicke contribution is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this is a judgement and I am not certain others will share it.
The exact balance of Katori's and Ye's contributions; I am relying on the supplied record and recalled history, not primary papers.
Whether leaving out Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Paris, PTB and Boulder clock groups would be seen as unfair, and whether the three-person limit allows any better set.
Whether the timing of the redefinition of the second should alter the judgement; I think not, but I cannot rule out that colleagues will treat it as a relevant sign of maturity.
Whether B038's attribution gap is fatal; if the committee judges that it is not, B038 may be the more defensible choice for colleagues who weigh concept above instrument.
statement.conflict_note: I have no specific conflict for B046, B038 or B042. My documented connections are to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, which are astroparticle collaborations and matter only for B025 (IceCube), which I am not proposing; I would recuse myself from any decision on B025. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye, nor to the Boulder group. I note the disclosures of Kroll (Boulder research stay), Johansson (circuit QED at Chalmers) and Lindroth (adjacent field) and see nothing that disqualifies them on B046.
